You are the pull-request quality gate. Find concrete merge-blocking defects without broadening scope into optional polish.

## What is already in front of you

This pull request's diff is in this conversation as a message, up to a size limit;
past that the message says it was truncated, and the files after the cut are ones
you have not seen. Its comments, and any earlier rounds on it, are there too. Call
`get_pr_diff` when you see that marker, or to look at a different pull
request — not to fetch what you already have.

So your reads are not for the diff. They are for everything the diff does not
contain, which is where the defects a diff cannot show you live: the callers of
something it deleted, the source of a file it regenerated, the other definitions
that name a server it renamed.

Count the review rounds from the comments in this conversation, and read the
submitted reviews as a second source rather than assuming there are none. The two
carry different rounds: an agent cannot submit one — every Atomaton agent shares
the identity that opened the pull request, and GitHub refuses a review from that
identity — so an agent's round is in the thread and absent from the review list,
while a person's review is submitted under their own identity and can be absent
from the thread. Count both. Where the two disagree, take the larger number and act
on it: a round counted twice costs nothing, and a round you dropped hides a loop
that is not converging. Five or more previous rounds means the loop is not
converging: write the remaining blockers and end with no directive line, so a
person is brought in.

An unverified "this is unused" is a blocker, not a saving. The author sees the
surface they were working on; a consumer in another file is exactly what they
cannot see.

## Mandatory checks

Run each of these that this diff triggers, and read the files they name. There is
no budget to weigh them against: each one covers a failure whose evidence is, by
definition, in a file the diff does not contain.

**Anything removed.** A diff that deletes a named thing — a YAML key, a list
entry, a file, an exported symbol, a config field — is safe only once you have
looked for its users yourself. Ask `search_code` what uses it, and read
every file that plausibly does. "Unused", "dead" or "never exposed" in a
description is a claim, not evidence. If you cannot search, the removal is
unverified — say so and return it.

**An agent definition or `tools.servers` changed.** Read every file under
`agent-definitions/`, not only the one in the diff. A name absent from
`tools.servers` is not a finding: Atomaton's own servers are not in the config and
cannot be, so in most repositories that section is empty, and the required check on
this pull request already runs `atoma validate` against its config and fails on a
name nothing provides. Spend the reads on what that check cannot judge — a server
this diff removes or renames while a definition still names it, an override that
pastes a whole shipped entry to change one field and so stops tracking the upstream
ones, and a server whose command is not `bun` without its package under
`tools.packages`.

**Generated output touched.** An edit made directly to a file a build produces is a
defect even when its content is correct, because the next build overwrites it and
the change is silently lost; require it in the source the generator reads. When the
project regenerates and commits that output itself, a diff carrying it is also a
defect. Establish which convention this project follows from its build
configuration rather than assuming.

**A workflow or the runner changed.** Trace the values a new step depends on. A
step that reads a file needs that file guaranteed present in the deployed tree, not
merely present in the branch where it was authored.

Decide from what you read, then act. Exactly one of these ends a run, and each is
the call named in it.
The three outcomes every role shares are in `Ending a run` above, and they apply here too.

| Situation | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| This node has no pull request | say so and end — there is nothing here to review |
| The review found merge-blocking defects | begin the response with the directive line naming the agent the body's `Opened by` line names (below), then list only the defects you have evidence for: for each, the failing behaviour, where it is, and the correction required |
| No defects, and `check_merge_readiness(pull_number=...)` reports ready | `merge_pr` |
| No defects, but it reports blockers | act by kind, using the table below, then end |

**Who a return goes to.** The pull request's body names the agent that opened it
in an `Opened by` line — `create_pr` writes it, at the end of the body, with a
link to the run. The findings go back to that agent: a directive line `/<name>`
on a line of its own, so the machinery dispatches them onto the work they are
about. When the body names no agent — a person opened the pull request — write
no directive line at all: report the findings and end. Nobody will be dispatched,
and that is the answer; the person takes them.

Call `check_merge_readiness` once you have a verdict, not before. It
answers who may merge and under what conditions, never whether the change is sound,
and a review that begins there becomes merge administration. What it reports are
the blockers GitHub and this project's rules impose: they are not review findings
and not yours to fix, and `merge_pr` returns the same list rather than
merging past them.

# `tools`

What an agent can reach, and under what watch. This section is
[additive](overview.md): everything below is added to the servers every run
already starts with.

## The servers every run starts with

| Server | What it is for | Credential |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `files` | Reads, searches and changes files in the work tree. Its tools are named `read`, `grep`, `glob`, `edit`, `write`, `list`, with no server prefix. | none |
| `files_readonly` | The same server with the three that write left out, for agents that must not change anything. | none |
| `shell` | Runs one foreground command. Guarded, and holds no credentials of its own. | none |
| `github` | Issues, pull requests, comments, and every Git mutation. | the run's GitHub token |
| `web` | Fetches a URL, and returns what it fetched. Searching the web is a skill rather than a tool — see [change or remove web fetching and search](tasks/change-or-remove-web-fetching-and-search.md). | none |
| `search` | Ranked search over your repository's issues and code. | the run's GitHub token |
| `atomaton` | Atomaton's own operations: sub-issues, handoffs, stopping a run. | the run's GitHub token |
| `attachments` | Probes GitHub's user-asset upload endpoint, the one `gh --attach` posts to, and publishes documents onto an orphan branch. `probe` reports the status and body the endpoint returned; only its `upload` mode stores anything, and a stored asset has no documented deletion. `publish_draft` puts drafts on a branch and returns a blob URL for each. | the run's GitHub token |
| `atomaton_env` | Rebuilding the run's environment, and concluding the run's own issue. | the run's GitHub token |
| `delegate` | Runs one small piece of work in a sub-run and returns what it found. Offers `delegate` and `delegate_large`. | the run's provider key |
| `delegate_readonly` | The same, with a sub-run that reads and searches and cannot change anything. Offers `delegate_readonly` and `delegate_readonly_large`. | the run's provider key |

Why five of them declare a credential rather than inheriting it, and why the
other four cannot see it, is
[how a credential reaches a tool](how-it-works/routing-a-credential.md).

`files_readonly` and `atomaton_env` are not separate implementations. Each is a
second entry for a server above with tools withheld — an allowlist, and
[a pattern with a reason](overview.md#one-server-two-entries).

`delegate` and `delegate_readonly` are the same arrangement for a different
reason. They are one program, `mcp/delegate.ts`, started with a different roster key.
What differs is what the sub-run may reach: `delegate` gives it `files` and `shell`,
`delegate_readonly` gives it `files_readonly` and nothing else. The pair exists
because a sub-run's servers must be a subset of its caller's — the reviewer holds
`files_readonly`, and a delegate that could write would put a writing server one
tool call away from an agent whose whole tool set says it cannot change anything.
Their definitions and tools files live under `.github/atomaton/delegates/`, **not**
under `agent-definitions/`, which is the namespace a person dispatches from. See
[delegating a piece of work](how-it-works/delegating-a-piece-of-work.md).

`delegates.yaml` in that directory is the roster: which server offers which folders.
It is under `.github/atomaton/` rather than in `tools/defaults.yaml` because which
delegates exist, what they are called and what each runs on is one decision in one
place — and a `model:` line is the thing a project most wants to change.

Each server offers two of them, and the difference is the model the folder names.
Nothing else differs, and they are the ones an agent is told to reach for first,
because a delegated task is the only place a free tier can be used at all: a
top-level run starts from the issue, every comment and the pull request's diff, which
exceeds the tier's per-request cap before the model says anything — while a delegate
is handed only the task its caller wrote, so the caller decides how much context it
carries. A task the tier refuses comes back as an error saying the prompt was too
big, which is an answer about the task's size; the agent narrows it or uses the other
folder for that one call.

**Which of the two is free is read from the `model:` line, not from the name.** A
folder whose model ends in `/free` is described to the caller as free, with a limit
shared across every agent on that tier, and the caller is told to try it and read a
refusal as an answer. Point the folder at another model and the description moves
with it, without an agent definition being edited — which is why the instruction
lives in the tool description rather than in an agent's prompt.

What each server's tools do in a run is in
[searching your repository's issues](how-it-works/searching-the-issues.md) and
[reading the web](how-it-works/reading-the-web.md).

`files` gives `read` an `offset` and a `limit` in lines, and a result that
stopped early names the offset to continue from. `read` also returns a picture as
a picture, so an agent whose definition sets
[`vision: true`](../agents/reference.md#vision) can look at a screenshot in the
repository; one without it gets a note saying the picture was withheld. `grep`
searches contents and takes `glob` to narrow which files and `context` for the
lines around a match; `glob` matches paths and never reads a file, so it does not
replace a grep — it answers where something is by name. There is no
`directory_tree`: it returns the whole tree, always, and there is no question
whose answer is the whole tree. `list` answers the ones there are.

`shell` is the one server that runs arbitrary commands, and therefore the one
that runs third-party code: a dependency's postinstall, a `setup.py`, a
`build.rs`. Those run with this server's privileges. `$HOME` is the runner's,
readable and **not** writable, the same for every tool — a write there fails
rather than appearing to work, because caches are redirected to a writable
directory by the environment the runner sets. Its `request_timeout_secs` is 3600,
which is a backstop for the server itself dying rather than a limit on the work:
the server enforces its own per-call limit and always answers.

## `tools.secrets`

Repository secrets the servers may reach, by name.

```yaml
tools:
  secrets:
    - SLACK_TOKEN
```

Naming a secret authorises the run to hold it. It does not deliver it to any
tool; the `env` on a server's own entry is the step that does, and
[the two are not one step](how-it-works/routing-a-credential.md).

**Four things fail the run** rather than being quietly dropped:

- a name that is not shaped like an environment variable (`SLACK_TOKEN`, not
  `slack_token` or `Slack-Token`)
- a name the run already uses for itself, such as `GH_TOKEN` or
  `OPENAI_API_KEY` — declaring one would replace the run's own value rather than
  add a credential
- the same name twice
- more than ten names, which is the number of slots the generated workflow
  carries; raising it needs a new release

A provider's `*_BASE_URL` may not be declared here either, for
[a different reason](../agents/boundaries.md).

Naming a secret the repository does not actually have is a warning rather than a
failure. The run itself is unaffected, and only the tool needing that value will
fail — with the reason already in the log.

Why this list is separate from a check's or a deployment's `secrets`, and why it
is in the config rather than in a repository variable, is
[what routing protects](boundaries.md).

## `tools.servers`

Servers of your own, and overrides of the ones Atomaton ships. It starts empty,
and what you write is **added to** the shipped set rather than standing in for
it.

One entry per server: `command`, `args`, `env`, `hooks`, `request_timeout_secs`,
and `settings` — the last being this project's own, stripped by the generator so
it never reaches the core. Everything else is the core's own tools-file format,

---
name: docs/design-doc
description: Load when a run must turn a document draft into issue-visible artifacts — publish the Markdown draft to the orphan branch, generate Office originals and a PDF on demand, publish them onto the same branch, and report the three blob URLs in the closing report.
---

# Publishing a design document: draft, originals, PDF

A document this run was asked to produce is delivered in three layers:

| Layer | Format | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 原稿 (the draft) | Markdown, tables as CSV sidecars | an orphan branch, via the `attachments` server's `publish_draft` |
| 原本 (the originals) | xlsx / docx / pptx | the same orphan branch — a second `publish_draft` |
| 閲覧用 (the reading copy) | PDF | the same branch, the same second call |

**The draft is the deliverable.** The originals and the PDF are how it is shown.
Every generation step below may fail; when one does, deliver what was produced
and say which layer is missing. A draft URL alone is a complete delivery of the
first layer — never hold the whole report hostage to LibreOffice.

## 1. The draft's contract

Write the draft as Markdown. A table is a separate `.csv` file next to the
draft, and the draft refers to it by its relative path (for example
`tables/layers.csv`) in the text where the table belongs. One CSV per table;
the first row is the header row. No other structure is required — the
converters read headings, list items and paragraphs, and pass everything else
through as text.

Lay the files out on the branch as `designs/<issue-number>/<slug>.md`, with
tables under `designs/<issue-number>/tables/`.

## 2. Publishing the draft — `publish_draft` (the `attachments` server)

Tool names here are bare: `publish_draft`, `probe`, `bash`, `read`. Every shipped
server is `unprefixed: true`, so a tool is called by its own name, and a name carrying
its server as a prefix is one no run has — the call fails as an unknown tool, and the
"not among your tools" branch below then reads as a deployment gap about a tool that is
right there. `<server>__<tool>` is the spelling for a server a project adds, not for
these.

```json
publish_draft({
  "files": [
    { "path": "draft/design.md", "target": "designs/111/design.md" },
    { "path": "draft/tables/layers.csv", "target": "designs/111/tables/layers.csv" }
  ],
  "message": "design draft: <title>"
})
```

- `path` is where the file is in this run's world (a checkout-relative path, or
  an absolute one under `/tmp`); `target` is where it goes on the branch.
- There is no `branch` argument. The branch is this repository's own setting —
  `tools.servers.attachments.settings.branch` in `.github/atomaton/config.yaml`,
  defaulting to `business-docs` — so a publish cannot be aimed at a branch the
  tool's guards do not see. If the request names a different branch, that is a
  settings change, not a tool argument: say so and stop.
- The branch is created as an **orphan** the first time (a root commit with no
  parent in the default branch's history) and fast-forwarded after, so one
  branch accumulates the documents' history and a document's diff stays
  readable — while the default branch's history stays clean.
- The run's own checkout is not touched: no switch, no worktree, no index
  change. Nothing you have staged or uncommitted can be lost by publishing.
- The tool returns `{ branch, commit_sha, files: [{ target, blob_url }] }`.
  The `blob_url` values are the draft URLs for the report.
- Publishing to the remote's default branch, or to the branch this run has
  checked out, is refused by the tool. That is the design, not an obstacle:
  a document lands on the orphan branch or nowhere.

**If `publish_draft` is not among your tools**, the running layer predates the
server's publish capability — record that, publish nothing, and
do not route around it. The shell cannot push (`git push` and every other
mutating git subcommand are refused there, by design), and `commit_and_push`
can only create a run's own work branch, which is exactly where a document
must not go. The draft leg waits for the deploy; run the rest of this
procedure and mark the draft URL as not yet available.

## 3. Generating the originals and the PDF — `generate.mjs`

Next to this skill file sits `generate.mjs`. Run it with bun (or node):

```bash
bun "${ATOMATON_MACHINERY_ROOT:-.}/.github/atomaton/skills/docs/generate.mjs" \
  <draft.md> --outdir <output-dir>
```

`ATOMATON_MACHINERY_ROOT` is where the run's own copy of the machinery is; the
`:-.` is the repository-relative fallback every other script here uses, so an
unset variable points at the checkout rather than at `/`.

It produces, into the output directory: `<slug>.docx` (the document), an xlsx
holding one sheet per referenced CSV, and `<slug>.pdf` (converted from the
docx). `--formats docx,xlsx,pdf` narrows it; `--pptx` adds a slide deck for a
draft that has one (xlsx→pdf and pptx→pdf are not supported; the PDF is of the
document).

**Dependencies are installed on demand, into a cache directory, and never into
`environment.setup_commands`.** The first run on a machine installs; every run
after that skips the install and says so in its output:

- python3 with a venv, and `pip install openpyxl python-docx` (plus
  `python-pptx` only when `--pptx` is asked) — seconds;
- LibreOffice, when no `soffice` is on the `PATH`: the release tarball is
  downloaded and the needed `.deb`s extracted under the cache with
  `dpkg-deb -x` — no root, tens of seconds, and the conversion itself is a
  couple of seconds;
- CJK fonts, best-effort (`fonts-noto-cjk`, extracted the same way), so a
  Japanese document does not convert to tofu. They are installed into
  `<cache>/atomaton-docgen/.fonts`, which is what LibreOffice reads as `~/.fonts`
  during the conversion. If this one fails the PDF still converts — the glyphs
  are the only casualty, and quality is not this procedure's concern.

The script's JSON output names every dependency `installed` or `cached` with
its seconds — quote that in the report when the run was the first on the
machine. A second run on the same machine says `cached` for every one of them
and takes under a second, which is the record that the install is on demand
rather than repeated. If an install fails, the script still exits with a summary
of what it did produce; deliver that, plus the draft URL, and say which layer is
missing.

## 4. Publishing the originals and the PDF — `publish_draft`, a second call

The generated files go onto the same branch the draft went to, by the same
tool — `publish_draft` again, with the output directory's files as `path` and
their place on the branch as `target`:

```json
publish_draft({
  "files": [
    { "path": "<output-dir>/design.docx", "target": "designs/111/design.docx" },
    { "path": "<output-dir>/design.xlsx", "target": "designs/111/design.xlsx" },
    { "path": "<output-dir>/design.pdf",  "target": "designs/111/design.pdf" }
  ],
  "message": "design originals and PDF: <title>"
})
```

- `target` carries no extension rule: the schema takes any file name
  (`DRAFT_FILE_SCHEMA`, in the attachments server), so the binaries go up as
  they are. One call per publication; the result's `blob_url` per file is what
  the report carries.
- A file on the branch is an ordinary git object — publishing over it replaces
  it, so a corrected original goes up as another call to the same `target`.
  That is a property of this route, not the reason it was chosen.
- **The upload route is closed, and measured so.** GitHub's user-asset upload
  endpoint refuses every body-bearing POST from the Actions token (`ghs_`),
  whatever the size or MIME type — a 20KB PDF, a 5-byte text and a 27MB random
  `.bin` all came back 404, while the same session's credential passed the
